item.title: See ya 2022 C++ x86-64 Linux TCP
item.description:
https://www.cnblogs.com/Solstice/p/3195397.html

“本书主要讲述采用现代 C++ 在 x86-64 Linux 上编写多线程 TCP 网络服务程序的主流常规技术”，封面印着“示范在多核时代采用现代 C++ 编写多线程 TCP 网络服务器的正规做法”。

很多教科书上介绍的一些做法是过时的（signal），一些是不推荐使用的（从外部终止线程、TCP OOB数据），一些是大多数情况下没必要使用的（内存池、lock-free 编程）。

多线程程序不要使用signal作为IPC。并且，在muduo-protorpc的示例中给出了Linux专有的signalfd(2)的用法，可以避免传统signal handler的常见陷阱，也更符合UNIX的“everything is a file”哲学。第4.4节说明不要从外部终止线程，因此也就不必去细究Pthreads cancellation point了。多线程程序最好不要fork()

daemon是过时的做法。因为daemon进程的父进程是init(1)，配置文件在本机，不便于多机统一监控与管理（第9.8节）。（注：如果是第三方标准的服务程序，又不需要经常升级或改配置重启，并且一旦崩溃，重启就能继续服务，那么做成 daemon 让init(1)接管是可以的，比如ntpd、sshd等。本书谈的是自己开发维护的服务程序。）另外，Java/Python/Go写的服务程序似乎也没有做成daemon的习惯，C++程序没有理由要特殊对待。补充一点，Linux的进程管理机制很落后（从UNIX继承而来），子进程退出的事件只能被父进程以SIGCHLD信号的方式收到（而且这个signal可能丢失），kill(pid) 也存在很多race condition（你怎么保证pid在kill之前的一瞬间还代表你想kill的那个进程，而不是一个新启动的进程？close(fd)就不会有这种 race condition。）。这些困难在用户态无法克服，只能修改内核，引入新的系统调用才能治本。例如 FreeBSD 9.0 引入了 pdfork()/pdkill() 等，将子进程变成文件描述符，这样就能用IO事件框架统一处理了，也符合UNIX的“everything is a file”哲学。但愿Linux内核也能尽快引入类似的系统调用，减轻程序员的负担。 这本书没有讲内存池，而是说明不是每个程序都要自己写内存池（§12.2.8）。这本书也没有把“避免内存碎片”挂在嘴边，而是论证为什么一般的程序不必在意它（§A.1.8）； 这本书只关注Linux，不考虑移植性。它推荐使用Linux专有的gettid()系统调用作为线程标识（第4.3节），而不是用pthread_self()。 这本书不讲POSIX中五花八门的定时函数，而专讲用Linux特有的timerfd来实现高精度定时（§7.8.2），因为它能方便地融入IO事件处理框架。

这本书只讲mutex和condition variable作为最基础的线程同步手段（第2章），并且我认为一个C++多线程程序代码里不应该直接出现pthread_mutex_lock之类的基本Pthreads调用。本书进一步建议只使用非递归的mutex（§2.1.1），这与某些网上文章的推荐正好相反。这本书第2.3节甚至建议不要使用读写锁和信号量（semaphore），因为一是容易用错，二是不见得能提高性能。mutex和condition variable是完备的，能实现多种更易用的同步设施，例如CountDownLatch和BlockingQueue。§12.8.3的代码展示了用BlockingQueue和ThreadPool控制并发度的手法，做到了“No locks. No condition variables. No callbacks.” 这本书不讲lock-free编程，因为编写可靠的lock-free代码并分析验证其正确性的难度远大于编写普通的使用mutex和condition variable的多线程代码，后者已经有了相当成熟的理论和工具。我认为lock-free不是每个多线程程序员应该掌握的技术，它投入高而用处少，可以适当了解，但不值得每个人都去深究。只需要少数人用它实现封装好的数据结构，像我这样的普通人就可以受益。 这本书只讲BSD Sockets作为进程间通信的手段，并且只用TCP长连接（§3.4）。这样就砍掉了pipe、FIFO、POSIX message queue、shared memory、STREAMS、UNIX domain socket等等内容，因为它们都只限本机进程间通信，无法扩展到多机。 网络编程方面（第6、7章），这本书不讲Sockets API的基本用法，而且代码中也不会直接使用它们。我认为在程序中直接使用 Sockets API是初学者的做法，当写一个新网络服务程序，如果一开始考虑的是怎么组织accept、read、epoll_wait等调用，这种做法无异于用铅笔刀锯大树，事倍功半，也不利于将来的功能扩展和维护。稍微像样点的公司都会用成熟的网络库（不一定开源），把网络编程的复杂性封装进去，暴露出良好易用的接口，让开发人员使用更高层的building blocks（消息传递或RPC）从功能的角度去设计程序，避免一次次反复掉到TCP网络编程的坑里。多个服务程序共享相同的基础库和事件处理框架的益处是显而易见的，一方面把网络编程的复杂性集中到一起，避免每个团队都去踏一遍坑；另一方面，基础库的bug修复与性能优化能惠及用到它的全部服务程序；最后，程序结构上的相似性让编程经验更加通用，多个服务程序在功能、性能、正确性等方面具有共性，能举一反三触类旁通，降低将来开发维护的成本。应该避免每个程序都另起炉灶，单独设计其IO事件处理结构。 这本书只讲非阻塞IO结合IO复用（IO-Multiplexing）这一种并发风格（归纳为三个半事件），并介绍在多线程下的扩展（one loop per thread）。IO复用方面，本书只讲level-trigger，不讲edge-trigger。一方面目前没有up to date的测试表明ET更快，相反，我认为LT在读取数据时可以节约一次read()调用（§8.7.2）；另一方面，LT模式更容易与其他第三方库结合（§7.15）。多线程程序管理并发socket fd有很多风格可供选择，例如epoll fd是多个线程共享一个（多对一）还是每个线程有自己的epoll fd（一对一），每个socket fd是只属于一个epoll fd（多对一）还是可以同时属于多个 epoll fd（多对多），每个socket fd是只能被固定的一个线程读写还是可以被多个线程读写（如果是后者，那么读写的时候是加锁还是使用ONESHOT）。以上不是每种都可行，本书也没有一一加以分析，而是建议使用one loop per thread这种适用性较强的风格，首先是正确性容易验证，其次是性能也能满足要求。 本书不讲IPv6，因为目前世界上最大的公司的服务机群也用不完一个私有A类地址（10.0.0.0/8）。本书不讲UDP，因为《Unix网络编程》已经讲得很好了。 这本书举的网络编程的例子不再是简单的echo服务，而是有格式（因此引入codec）、多连接之间会交换数据的网络程序，更接近业务场景，也借机讲解如何避免TCP网络编程的常见陷阱。并且在示例代码中给出了分布式单词计数、多机求中位数等稍微复杂一点的程序。 在C++方面，这本书没有介绍动态链接库热更新这种“高级”技术，而是说明，在分布式系统中，为了部署方便，应该从源码编译全部的库，与主程序链接为一个standalone的可执行文件，以减小对运行环境的依赖

https://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_80_0/more/getting_started/unix-variants.html https://www.boost.org/doc/libs/

Thanks! Ali ————– next part ————– An HTML attachment was scrubbed… URL: http://lists.opencompute.org/pipermail/opencompute-onie/attachments/20160817/7c74ed58/attachment.html

Hi Ali,

In order for UEFI Secure Boot to be an option, hardware vendors must include a TPM (preferably 2.0 or higher). At the moment, there are only a couple of devices that have a TPM present.

From banther at gmail.com Thu Aug 18 01:47:52 2016 From: banther at gmail.com (Mark Pearson) Date: Thu, 18 Aug 2016 01:47:52 +0000 Subject: [Opencompute-onie] ONIE UEFI Secure Boot In-Reply-To: <D3DA3B34.58E0%aaldhahe@ciena.com> References: <D3D9FF88.58D7%aaldhahe@ciena.com> <CAMgwifxeRq1whKG8Fe+qjA5KDDWFC-zHF_vW2dAsRS7MEe6Pzw@mail.gmail.com> <D3DA3B34.58E0%aaldhahe@ciena.com> Message-ID: CANfa5DYWrHovnyDCYU4d_q0DLabM0tpSKKM_6n0kYPKvz3Mzbw@mail.gmail.com

My $0.02 having spent some time looking at this..I am interested in to see what others think

To boot ONIE with secure boot enabled you are going to have to have a signed ONIE grub image as a minimum - and to do that in the community build you’d have to put your private key into the ONIE repository and that probably isn’t wise :)

You could sign an ONIE grubx64.efi and do your own special private ONIE release (not sure how that sits with the community…but it’s technically doable)

If you go this route I don’t think the ONIE grub currently has the patches to support secure boot (assuming you want to use the standard linux efi shim for also authenticating your kernel because what’s the point of secure boot if you don’t do that). You also hit headaches with how you release that grub executable (do you sign all the modules or do a standalone grub?). You likely have to mess around with the ONIE updater steps, build steps etc - not trivial :)

I don’t know if these changes are of interest to the rest of the community as it ultimately leads to a locked down private ONIE and it all seems somewhat counter-intuitive to me: now nobody can really load on their OS except for the key owner as they won’t have the key to sign images. This seems to defeat the point of ONIE.

What I think makes sense for customers that are security conscious is:

  • Have UEFI ONIE and a system that has secure boot capability but with secure boot disabled
  • Provide customers with a certificate to load your key into the UEFI firmware database (you could pre-load on your own hardware if you are a HW and SW vendor)
  • Provide your ONIE OS installer which installs signed bootloader, kernel etc to work with secure boot when enabled

With this a customer can then enable secure boot once they have installed your secure OS and your key. The big downside is I think enabling secure boot itself is a manual process and requires going into the firmware menu. I’ve not found a way to be able to enable it from linux but my experience in this area is virtually nil though - maybe it’s possible? It would be neat if it’s possible but I suspect it wouldn’t be by design

Note: the above is my opinion only. I’m also not an expert in this area - I’ve just been actively tinkering recently with secure boot to see what it can do and the email thread grabbed my interest

Mark

PS - FWIW I don’t think TPM is a requirement for secure boot - it helps add a measured boot component to your secure implementation but isn’t actively required. I’m happy to be corrected ;)

Mark Pearson wrote:

My $0.02 having spent some time looking at this..I am interested in to see what others think

To boot ONIE with secure boot enabled you are going to have to have a signed ONIE grub image as a minimum - and to do that in the community build you’d have to put your private key into the ONIE repository and that probably isn’t wise :)

You could sign an ONIE grubx64.efi and do your own special private ONIE release (not sure how that sits with the community…but it’s technically doable)?

If you go this route I don’t think the ONIE grub currently has the patches to support secure boot (assuming you want to use the standard linux efi shim for also authenticating your kernel because what’s the point of secure boot if you don’t do that). You also hit headaches with how you release that grub executable (do you sign all the modules or do a standalone grub?). You likely have to mess around with the ONIE updater steps, build steps etc - not trivial :)?

At a past company, the legal department expressed their opinion that this kind of thing would be a violation of GPL v2 for grub, because it prevents booting a kernel of the end-user’s choice.

Some kind of override would have to be allowed to live within the GPL.

The lockdown of ONIE would almost certainly be a GPL violation as well, if that legal opinion was correct.

Again, an override would have to be provided (as you suggest).

However, once anything can be booted that is not verified through secure boot, that gives the ability to bypass/alter the TPM, BIOS, grub, etc., thereby making the system no longer secure (or at least, the potential for not being secure). Sort of makes the whole thing pointless…

Dave Olson olson at cumulusnetworks.com

From banther at gmail.com Mon Aug 29 12:30:20 2016 From: banther at gmail.com (Mark Pearson) Date: Mon, 29 Aug 2016 12:30:20 +0000 Subject: [Opencompute-onie] ONIE UEFI Secure Boot In-Reply-To: 20160818021611.GA12998@cumulusnetworks.com References: <D3D9FF88.58D7%aaldhahe@ciena.com> <CAMgwifxeRq1whKG8Fe+qjA5KDDWFC-zHF_vW2dAsRS7MEe6Pzw@mail.gmail.com> <D3DA3B34.58E0%aaldhahe@ciena.com> CANfa5DYWrHovnyDCYU4d_q0DLabM0tpSKKM_6n0kYPKvz3Mzbw@mail.gmail.com 20160818021611.GA12998@cumulusnetworks.com Message-ID: <CANfa5Db8ZRM+g_DrWTUODUw=2NJGk8dq4g70SURNFKL7gzRO6g@mail.gmail.com>

Hi Dave,

(sorry for the slow reply - summer holidays ;))

Specifically on this bit: “However, once anything can be booted that is not verified through secure boot, that gives the ability to bypass/alter the TPM, BIOS, grub, etc., thereby making the system no longer secure (or at least, the potential for not being secure). Sort of makes the whole thing pointless… “

My take is if a customer enables secure boot and then protects their switch (physically and by password protecting the firmware configuration) then secure boot is a good way of securing the switch after the fact. It assumes that the UEFI firmware isn’t compromised but covers everything from then on. Am I missing something?

I did think about this a bit more and can see two options that could work.

Option 1: Nothing new required. The HW is shipped with ONIE available and if a customer wants to use secure boot with SW that is signed they have to be aware that they need to enable secure boot in the firmware menu and load in the key to verify the signatures. It sucks there are manual steps but that’s the price of security.

Option 2: We add some extra bits to ONIE - specifically building the shim.efi bootloader and signing the shim, grub and kernel with a key of the builders choosing (presumably local). With this if you have a key you could then build a “secure ONIE” which you could release yourself (nobody else could build it). This ONIE would boot on a switch with secure boot enabled (assuming the key is installed of course). A vendor which provides both HW and SW could use this to ship a secure switch with both their software and ONIE. If a customer wants to install an alternate OS they will have to disable secure boot (or install the alternate OS key). I guess potentially a HW vendor could also choose to provide a signing service but I’m going to guess that nobody would be interested in that. A truly security aware customer should verify that their key database only contains the key they require and that secure boot is enabled - so some manual steps are required anyway which makes me wonder if it’s worth the effort of going this route

Would option 2 be of interest to anyone else? Does it go against the ONIE community open approach? I know at Lenovo (where I work) that we would probably use this approach if it was available so if it’s of interest I can put in the effort to make the changes. I’d only want to do it if it was likely to be useful to others too - I personally don’t like the idea of a locked down ONIE….it feels ethically icky :) I can be convinced otherwise if it is of general interest and would not be purely selfish.

Thoughts? Mark

On Wed, 17 Aug 2016 at 22:19 Dave Olson wrote:

Mark Pearson wrote:

My $0.02 having spent some time looking at this..I am interested in to see what others think

To boot ONIE with secure boot enabled you are going to have to have a signed ONIE grub image as a minimum - and to do that in the community build you’d have to put your private key into the ONIE repository and that probably isn’t wise :)

You could sign an ONIE grubx64.efi and do your own special private ONIE release (not sure how that sits with the community…but it’s technically doable)

If you go this route I don’t think the ONIE grub currently has the patches to support secure boot (assuming you want to use the standard linux efi shim for also authenticating your kernel because what’s the point of secure boot if you don’t do that). You also hit headaches with how you release that grub executable (do you sign all the modules or do a standalone grub?). You likely have to mess around with the ONIE updater steps, build steps etc - not trivial :)

At a past company, the legal department expressed their opinion that this kind of thing would be a violation of GPL v2 for grub, because it prevents booting a kernel of the end-user’s choice.

Some kind of override would have to be allowed to live within the GPL.

The lockdown of ONIE would almost certainly be a GPL violation as well, if that legal opinion was correct.

Again, an override would have to be provided (as you suggest).

However, once anything can be booted that is not verified through secure boot, that gives the ability to bypass/alter the TPM, BIOS, grub, etc., thereby making the system no longer secure (or at least, the potential for not being secure). Sort of makes the whole thing pointless…

Dave Olson olson at cumulusnetworks.com

Hi Mark,

I think generally “Option 2” you describe below is the way forward for Secure Boot and ONIE. I think a HW vendor “owns” the platform and is best positioned to sign and provide ONIE.

I am in the process of documenting some Secure Boot workflows for ONIE, including things like:

  • Manufacturing work flow. How is the firmware installed? How is ONIE installed? What needs to be done here.

  • OS installers. How will OS installers interact with a Secure Boot ONIE system?

  • Roll your own end users. How will fully security conscious folks interact with the systems?

Cheers, Curt
